docs.title: Signed Webhook Receiver
docs.text:
Verify. Trust. Process.

A lightweight and secure webhook receiver built with FastAPI that verifies incoming webhook requests using RSA SHA-256 digital signatures.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Signed Webhook Receiver is a secure webhook gateway that validates incoming requests before processing them.

The receiver never trusts incoming messages unless the provided signature can be verified using the configured RSA public key.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Sender
  |
  | Create webhook payload
  |
  | Sign data with RSA private key
  |
  v
Webhook Receiver
  |
  | Verify signature with RSA public key
  |
  +-- Valid signature ---> Process data
  |
  +-- Invalid signature -> Reject request

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• RSA SHA-256 signature verification
  • RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signing support
  • FastAPI + Uvicorn
  • Docker ready
  • Traefik compatible
  • Public key based verification
  • Lightweight microservice architecture

docs.title: Request Flow
docs.text:
The sender creates a payload containing:

  • data — webhook event information
  • sign — Base64 encoded RSA signature

docs.title: Example:
docs.text:
{
  "sign": "BASE64_SIGNATURE",
  "data": {
      "event": "payment.completed",
      "id": 123
  }
}

docs.title: Supported Languages
docs.text:
Webhook senders can be implemented using:

  • Python
  • JavaScript / Node.js
  • Go

Each implementation must follow the same signing protocol to generate compatible signatures.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
This project uses asymmetric cryptography:

  • The sender owns the private key
  • The receiver only stores the public key
  • Incoming requests are accepted only after signature verification

The private key must never be shared with the receiver.

docs.title: Production Recommendations
docs.text:
For production environments:

  • Always use HTTPS
  • Protect your private keys
  • Add timestamps to prevent replay attacks
  • Validate webhook payloads before processing
  • Use canonical JSON before signing

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Webhook endpoint:

POST /api/v1/webhook

Request body:

{
  "sign": "BASE64_SIGNATURE",
  "data": {
    "event": "payment.completed",
    "id": 123
  }
}

Successful response:

{
  "status": "ok"
}

Invalid signatures are rejected.

docs.title: Go Webhook Sender
docs.text:
This example shows how to generate a signed webhook payload using Go.

The sender uses:

  • Go standard crypto packages
  • RSA private key
  • SHA-256 hashing
  • PKCS#1 v1.5 padding
  • Base64 encoded signature

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "crypto"
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/rsa"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "crypto/x509"
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/pem"
    "fmt"
    "os"
)


func main() {

    data := `{"event":"payment.completed","id":123}`


    privateKeyData, err := os.ReadFile(
        "private.pem",
    )

    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }


    block, _ := pem.Decode(
        privateKeyData,
    )


    privateKey, err := x509.ParsePKCS1PrivateKey(
        block.Bytes,
    )

    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }


    hash := sha256.Sum256(
        []byte(data),
    )


    signature, err := rsa.SignPKCS1v15(
        rand.Reader,
        privateKey,
        crypto.SHA256,
        hash[:],
    )

    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }


    sign := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(
        signature,
    )


    payload := fmt.Sprintf(
        `{
            "sign":"%s",
            "data":{
                "event":"payment.completed",
                "id":123
            }
        }`,
        sign,
    )


    fmt.Println(payload)
}

Example request:

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The receiver verifies the signature using the RSA public key. The data used for signing must match the receiver’s canonical JSON format.

docs.title: The signing process
docs.text:
Data
 |
 v
Canonical JSON
 |
 v
SHA-256 hash
 |
 v
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5
 |
 v
Base64 signature

The private key stays on the sender side.

The receiver only requires the public key for verification.

docs.title: JavaScript Webhook Sender
docs.text:
This example shows how to generate a signed webhook payload using Node.js.

The private key must only exist on the backend/server side. Never expose the RSA private key in browser JavaScript.

The sender uses:

  • Node.js built-in crypto module
  • RSA SHA-256
  • PKCS#1 v1.5 padding
  • Base64 encoded signature

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Node.js 18+

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import crypto from "node:crypto";
import fs from "node:fs";


const privateKey = fs.readFileSync(
    "private.pem"
);


const data = {
    event: "payment.completed",
    id: 123
};


const message = JSON.stringify(
    {
        event: data.event,
        id: data.id
    }
);


const signature = crypto.sign(
    "RSA-SHA256",
    Buffer.from(message, "utf-8"),
    {
        key: privateKey,
        padding: crypto.constants.RSA_PKCS1_PADDING
    }
);


const sign = signature.toString(
    "base64"
);


const payload = {
    sign,
    data
};


console.log(payload);

docs.title: Python Webhook Sender
docs.text:
This example shows how to generate a signed webhook payload using Python.

The sender uses:

  • RSA private key
  • SHA-256 hashing
  • PKCS#1 v1.5 padding
  • Base64 encoded signature

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Install the required package:

pip install cryptography

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import json
import base64

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding


data = {
    "event": "payment.completed",
    "id": 123
}


message = json.dumps(
    data,
    separators=(",", ":"),
    sort_keys=True
).encode("utf-8")


signature = private_key.sign(
    message,
    padding.PKCS1v15(),
    hashes.SHA256()
)


sign = base64.b64encode(
    signature
).decode("ascii")


payload = {
    "sign": sign,
    "data": data
}

docs.title: Send Webhook
docs.text:
Send the generated payload to:

POST https://your-domain.com/api/v1/webhook

Example request:

{
  "sign": "BASE64_SIGNATURE",
  "data": {

    "id": 123

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The JSON serialization must be identical between sender and receiver.

The following configuration is used:

  • Sorted keys
  • Compact separators
  • UTF-8 encoding

The receiver verifies the signature using the public key.
